title: Payroll that does not fit the head count
question: Does the pay bill on each return fit the number of employees on the same return, and what share of all pay goes to the people at the top?
finding: The middle organization among 427 with at least three employees spends $61,213 in salaries and benefits per employee counted. 13 report a payroll of $100,000 or more with no employees, and 0 report five or more employees with no payroll. 21 come out at two and a half times their peers or more, led by Applied Technology Council at $253,545 for each of 7 employees; 15 with twenty or more employees come out at a fifth or less. At 20 with five or more employees, officers and key employees take 40% or more of all pay, and at 20 their pay rose by a quarter or more while programme spending fell by a tenth or more.
how: From the latest full return of each organization: salaries, other compensation and benefits (Part I line 15), the number of employees (Part I line 5, the count of wage statements for the calendar year ending in the tax year), and pay to current officers, directors, trustees and key employees (Part IX line 5). Cost per employee is the first divided by the second. Peers are organizations whose largest City funder is the same department, where at least eight have three or more employees; otherwise all organizations. The last pattern compares the first return showing $50,000 or more of officer pay with the latest, at least two years apart. The largest City funder is the department that paid the organization most in the Controller's nonprofit-spending table, which counts contracted services.
limits: The employee count is everyone who received a wage statement in the calendar year, including a person paid for one day, a stipended youth or a summer worker, so cost per head is low wherever such programmes are large and that pattern alone is not counted as a tripped test. It is high where staff are few and senior, where doctors or lawyers are employed, or where a staffing firm or parent body employs most workers. Whom to list as an officer or key employee is partly a judgement, and adding a name raises the line without anyone being paid more. Emergency programmes that ended after 2021 pull programme spending down for reasons unrelated to pay. A pattern here is a reason to ask for the audited statements, not a finding.
